    15	
    16	# Lead PM
    17	
    18	You hold the role where intent enters the shop and where the product's
    19	outcome is answered for. You turn what an originator — whoever expresses intent at the
    20	product's edge — asks for into a recorded *framing* — the problem the shop takes the request to be
    21	about and the outcome it serves — and you check what the PO role makes
    22	from that framing against it. The product authority holds this role in
    23	person; that is the role's authority. Agents assist the role's
    24	activities (see Interfaces); the frontmatter contracts those agents,
    25	and the person holding the role is bound by the definitions, not by
    26	the tool list.
    27	
    28	**Standard of judgment:** outcomes, not outputs — you frame a problem
    29	to solve, never a feature to build. You engage an originator's
    30	statements as an interlocutor and record convergence rather than
    31	inferring it. Material reaches you decidable — a screen verdict, a decision brief,
    32	or an ask (a question a definition cannot answer, sent with a
    33	proposed default) — or it goes back to the role that sent it with the
    34	missing criterion named.
    35	
    36	**Accountable for:**
    37	- The initiative for each problem worth solving, opening with the
    38	  framing of its intent: the originator, the expressed outcome, the
    39	  problem taken to be worth solving, and the contract — product or
    40	  operational — it entered through; the rest of the initiative — one
    41	  measured outcome, appetite and no-gos — drafted by the assisting
    42	  agent and decided here; screened by the cold reviewer as the check
    43	  of record.
    44	- The value and viability judgment on every candidate problem: whether
    45	  it is worth solving and whether the product can sustain the solution.
    46	- The check on the product-owner (PO) role's output — features,
    47	  decision records, backlog order — against the framing, under criteria the definitions state: a
    48	  pass, a fail with the criterion named, or a definition change where
    49	  the criteria proved insufficient.
    50	- Roadmap priority: which framed problems come first, recorded with
    51	  reasons.
    52	- Convergence of each discovery conversation recorded on its anchor
    53	  (see the [glossary](../glossary.md)).
    54	- The provenance chain: any activity traceable to its originating
    55	  expression without ambiguity, and every decision applied to the
    56	  governed artifacts it changes with a Document History entry.
    57	
    58	**Domain (exclusive):** the framing of intent — what the shop takes an
    59	expression to be asking for is decided by this role alone.
    60	
    61	**Decision rights.**
    62	- *Decides:* the framing (exclusive); and, as the accountable role,
    63	  value and viability, roadmap priority, and whether the PO's output
    64	  passes its check — each recorded with its reasons and open to another
    65	  role's evidence.
    66	- *Recommends:* scope changes to the PO with reasons; the outcome a
    67	  shape must serve to the solutions architect.
    68	- *Resolves:* a conflict between this role's framing and another
    69	  role's domain, recorded on the affected artifacts; no role overrides this
    70	  one's framing.
    71	- *Never decides:* feasibility and the stack (the
    72	  [solutions architect](lead-solutions-architect.md)'s);
    73	  authorship of acceptance scenarios and backlog order within the
    74	  framing (the PO's); usability (the
    75	  [product designer](lead-product-designer.md)'s); how a
    76	  Bounded Context builds a behavior (the BC-shop's).
    77	
    78	**Admissible evidence:** the originator's own words, recorded;
    79	discovery-conversation anchors; measured outcomes of shipped work; a
    80	screen verdict — a cold reviewer's judgment against a named criteria
    81	set (a fitness set, a guideline, or the framing itself). Not authoritative: a stakeholder's feature list read as a
    82	requirement; the PO's backlog read as the product's intent; the
    83	role's own reading of every artifact in place of a stated criterion.
    84	
    85	**Interfaces:**
    86	- Originators: intent in; the recorded framing back.
    87	- The PO role: framed intent and its outcome out; features, decision
    88	  records, backlog order, and scope questions in for the check.
    89	- The solutions architect role: framed problem and outcome out;
    90	  feasibility verdict, technical risks, and questions in.
    91	- The product designer role: framed problems and outcomes out;
    92	  usability evidence, prototypes, and observed user needs in.
    93	- Assisting agents: each assisted activity's process names what the
    94	  agent prepares and what this role decides.
    95	- Asks from any role: answered here, and a recurring ask becomes a
    96	  definition change.
    97	
    98	**Knowledge and skills:** product discovery and interviewing; the
    99	four product risks — value, usability, feasibility, viability — and
   100	which role answers for each (value and viability here; feasibility
   101	with the solutions architect; usability with the product designer); the shop's
   102	definition corpus (every activity run through the basis); the
   103	[stakeholder-presentation](../processes/stakeholder-presentation.md)
   104	and [discovery-conversation](../processes/discovery-conversation.md)
   105	processes; the [working principle set](../principles.md) every
   106	activity runs under.
   107	
   108	**Anti-rationalization:**
   109	- "I'll just read the scenarios myself." → A check without a stated
   110	  criterion is a read, not a check; the criterion is the missing
   111	  definition.
   112	- "The PO knows what I meant." → A framing is recorded or it does not
   113	  exist.
   114	- "This feature is obviously worth it." → Value is a judgment with
   115	  evidence named; the feature list is not the evidence.
   116	- "It's infeasible, so the framing is wrong." → Infeasible returns the
   117	  problem for re-framing; it does not decide what is worth solving.
   118	- "I'll decide the how while I'm here." → The how belongs to the
   119	  architect and the shops; deciding it here removes their check.
   120

    13	# Artifact type: initiative
    14	
    15	## Identity and ancestry
    16	
    17	- **Type:** `initiative` — the product-level problem artifact: one
    18	  problem worth solving, stated for the product, not for any Bounded
    19	  Context, with the outcome it serves and how that outcome will be
    20	  measured, the appetite the product will spend on it, what it will

    44	
    45	`type: initiative`, `id`, `status`, `version`, `name`, `owner`
    46	(`lead-pm`), `created`, `updated`. `approved` does not apply; the
    47	lifecycle below stands in. Status values and their writers: `proposed`
    48	(the PM role, on drafting — the framed-but-unbet state; a request
    49	declined at this stage becomes `cancelled`, so the record of what was
    50	declined survives); `planned` (the authority's go/no-go in a review,

    52	the first feature derived from it passing); `completed` (the
    53	`reconcile-and-close` process, when the last delivery under it is
    54	reconciled and the measure is recorded against its target);
    55	`cancelled` (the PM role's decision in a review, with the reason
    56	recorded, from any state).
    57	
    58	## Required sections
    59	
    60	1. **Framing** — the originator (who expressed the intent, in their own
    61	   words, quoted), the problem taken to be worth solving, the outcome
    62	   it serves, and the contract — product or operational — it entered
    63	   through. The PM role's exclusive decision.
    64	2. **For whom** — who has the problem and how the product will know
    65	   the outcome was reached: one measure with its current condition and
    66	   its target.
    67	3. **Appetite** — how much the product will spend on it — time, or
    68	   capacity — as a bound the features stay within; and the no-gos: what
    69	   this initiative will not do, each with its reason.
    70	4. **Feasibility and usability** — the solutions architect role's
    71	   feasibility verdict with its reasons, and, where the problem has an
    72	   interaction, the product designer role's usability evidence or the
    73	   hypothesis it stands on; each attached before the go/no-go or
    74	   marked "not yet" with the ask that requests it.
    75	5. **Decomposition** — attached by the solutions architect role: the
    76	   Bounded Contexts the initiative touches, the relationship kind of
    77	   each contract between them it relies on, and the cross-context flow
    78	   in one place — the saga or process manager that will carry it, or
    79	   "none" when the contexts need no flow between them. "Not yet" until
    80	   attached.
    81	6. **Features** — the features made from it, by id, as they are made;
    82	   empty until the first.
    83	
    84	## Rules
    85	
    86	- The framing is written here and nowhere else; a check that names the
    87	  framing as a criterion reads this section.
    88	- An initiative names no solution and no interface form; naming the
    89	  interaction types the outcome must hold on is a what.
    90	- An initiative touching more than one Bounded Context is counted, per
    91	  period, as the boundary signal the solutions architect role reads.
    92	- A decision the initiative records — the go/no-go, a cancellation —
    93	  is carried by a product decision record linked from the Document
    94	  History.
    95	
    96	## Commitment (Definition of Done)
    97	
    98	An initiative is done — able to be bet on — when it has passed the
    99	cold reviewer's screen against its fitness set, its feasibility
   100	verdict is attached, and its measure has a current condition and a
   101	target. **Consequence on failure:** it stays `proposed` with the

11	    10	---
12	    11	
13	    12	# Base writing style
14	    13	
15	    14	These rules apply to everything written for a human reader, regardless of
16	    15	document type. Document types add a format layer on top of this base; they
17	    16	never override it.
18	    17	
19	    18	## Goal
20	    19	
21	    20	The reader gets the point of any paragraph in one read, any section in 30
22	    21	seconds, and the whole document in two minutes. Write for the first read.
23	    22	
24	    23	## Lead with the point
25	    24	
26	    25	At every scale, state the conclusion first and the support after.
27	    26	
28	    27	- A document opens with what it found or decided, not how it got there.
29	    28	- A section opens with its main claim, then evidence.
30	    29	- A paragraph opens with its point, then elaboration.
31	    30	
32	    31	If a document type defines a structure, that structure is just this rule
33	    32	applied to that type. If no structure is defined, use this rule to invent
34	    33	one.
35	    34	
36	    35	## Detail placement
37	    36	
38	    37	Precision serves the point; it never precedes it. Formal specification
39	    38	language, methods, raw data, scoring tables, and citations go after the
40	    39	claim they support — or in an appendix. The body is for understanding.
41	    40	
42	    41	## Sentences
43	    42	
44	    43	- One idea per sentence.
45	    44	- Active voice, with a named actor: "Reviewers delete unlinked checks,"
46	    45	  not "Unlinked checks are subject to deletion."
47	    46	- Prefer the short common word: "use" not "utilize," "end" not
48	    47	  "terminate," "before" not "prior to."
49	    48	
50	    49	## Terminology
51	    50	
52	    51	- Never use a metaphor as a technical term. If a word describes a thing
53	    52	  by what it resembles instead of what it literally does, replace it with
54	    53	  the literal description. Test: could a competent reader from outside
55	    54	  the team work out the meaning from the words alone? If not, rewrite.
56	    55	- Banned words. Never use these, in any form:
57	    56	  - "load-bearing" → say "other work depends on it" or "critical to
58	    57	    operations"
59	    58	  - "surface" (as in context surface, config surface) → say "input,"
60	    59	    "source," or "channel"
61	    60	  - "seam" → say "boundary" or "integration point"
62	    61	  - "scar tissue" → describe the actual problem, e.g. "an unreviewed
63	    62	    workaround that was never removed"

107	    12	# Glossary
108	    13	
109	    14	## How the list combines
110	    15	
111	    16	The defined-term list is this glossary combined with every schema element
112	    17	name. Per the `use-defined-terms` principle, a writer choosing between
113	    18	terms uses one of these when one fits.
114	    19	
115	    20	## Terms
116	    21	
117	    22	- **artifact type** — a named, schema-defined document type (e.g.
118	    23	  `decision-brief`); the term the schema registry uses. Not "kind".
119	    24	- **data type** — a named, schema-defined structure that is not a
120	    25	  human-readable document (e.g. `review`); passed between process steps.
121	    26	- **simple type** — a JSON Schema primitive (`string`, `integer`,
122	    27	  `boolean`, `array`, `object`), usable inline without registration.
123	    28	- **typedef** — the single source a type is generated from; templates and
124	    29	  schema fragments are its renderings (owned by shopsystem-knowledge).
125	    30	- **schema** — the machine-checkable shape of a type: fields, types,
126	    31	  enums, required sections.
127	    32	- **process definition** — the source of truth for a process: header
128	    33	  (purpose, outcomes, roles), data section, steps section.
129	    34	- **step** — one unit of a process: an agent step (carries a prompt) or a
130	    35	  runtime step (carries `set`, `run`, or `branches`; no prose).
131	    36	- **rendering** — a generated output of a definition (a skill, a
132	    37	  diagram, a template); never edited by hand, never the source of truth.
133	    38	- **guiding statement** — an optional header element of a process
134	    39	  definition that directs judgment across the whole process; compiled
135	    40	  into every rendering.
136	    41	- **fitness set** — judged (never executed) Given/When/Then scenarios
137	    42	  scoring an artifact type's quality.
138	    43	- **guideline** — prose quality rules for an artifact type, each with a
139	    44	  test, a criterion, and a yes/no decision.
140	    45	- **role** — a named capability contract and set of accountabilities,
141	    46	  assigned by process steps to whoever fills it; sequencing lives in
142	    47	  process definitions, not roles.
143	    48	- **principle** — a standing rule about how we work: name, statement,
144	    49	  rationale, implications (see the principles document's opening
145	    50	  definition).
146	    51	- **seed layer** — the hand-approved definitions the regress terminates
147	    52	  at: the principle set plus one typedef per definition document type.
148	    53	- **owner** — the role that approves changes to a definition; named in
149	    54	  every definition's frontmatter.
150	    55	- **definition chain** — the six linked definitions of good for one
151	    56	  artifact type; required before instances are authored or rewritten.
152	    57	- **keeper** — a corpus record whose action is keep-rewrite; rewritten
153	    58	  forward through its type's approved chain, never used as-is.
154	    59	- **rewrite-forward** — the default for keepers: re-author to the
155	    60	  approved standard; repair-in-place only for records already at the bar.
156	    61	- **rebaseline** — Phase 1 of the re-founding arc: the active tree comes
157	    62	  to hold only chain-conforming records; retired mass moves to the
158	    63	  archive.
159	    64	- **scope** (of a principle set) — the level the set governs and whose
160	    65	  context it loads into: working (every activity), architecture (the
161	    66	  designed system), or experience (the product's interactions).
162	    67	- **transcript** — the runtime log of turns; unscoped, not a governed
163	    68	  artifact, never loaded into context.
164	    69	- **conversation** — a scoped, bounded discussion attached to exactly one
165	    70	  anchor; every conversation belongs to a process.
166	    71	- **anchor** — the governed record a conversation attaches to: a session
167	    72	  record, a review record, or a work item; carries the conversation's
168	    73	  state across transcript boundaries.
169	    74	- **conversation type** — discovery (anchor: a session record), review
170	    75	  (anchor: a review record and its outcomes), or work (anchor: a work
171	    76	  item).
172	    77	- **session record** — the anchor record of a discovery conversation:
173	    78	  outcome, produced and revised lists, open threads, select quotes.
174	    79	- **review** — one bounded conversation in which the authority decides
175	    80	  on presented material. Replaces "sitting".
176	    81	- **review record** — the anchor record of a review: the material
177	    82	  presented and the outcomes applied; each decision traces in the
178	    83	  changed artifacts' Document History, never in a standing ledger.
179	    84	- **park** — the failsafe for work that cannot pass review within its
180	    85	  round cap: set aside with a filed finding.
181	    86	- **round cap** — the declared maximum review rounds before a loop's
182	    87	  failsafe exit fires.
183	    88	- **action** — the approved choice for one record: keep-rewrite, keep,
184	    89	  retire, or terminal, with its target.
185	    90	- **authority-call** — a row marker on a migration-plan row awaiting a
186	    91	  decision from the authority; not an action — the row has no effect and
187	    92	  is out of scope for any run until ruled.
188	    93	- **action table** — the table of records and their actions; approved row
189	    94	  by row or in blocks at a review. Drives any bulk record change.
190	    95	- **close-out** — the mechanical execution of the migration plan's
191	    96	  pre-decided retire and terminal actions: snapshot, delete, archive
192	    97	  move, a loud post-check, and the branch promotion; no review loop.
193	    98	  All stages run consecutively at cut-over.
194	    99	- **snapshot tag** — the annotated git tag (`pre-migration`) on `main`'s
195	   100	  pre-execution commit, preserving the full corpus for terminal-recovery;
196	   101	  after close-out a terminal record exists only there.
197	   102	- **migration plan** — the rebaseline's action table plus the order of
198	   103	  the per-type migration runs. Replaces "rebaseline bill".
199	   104	- **run** — one execution of a process, anchored to a work item; states:
200	   105	  running, held, done, cancelled.
201	   106	- **hold** — a run state: paused with its step and data preserved in its
202	   107	  anchor, by inactivity or by an ask; a held run is resumed or
203	   108	  cancelled, never dropped.
204	   109	- **checkpoint** — updating a conversation's anchor when a transcript
205	   110	  ends mid-conversation; a checkpoint is not a close.
206	   111	- **branched conversation** — a conversation run as a sub-process of
207	   112	  another run; its anchor records the parent (`branched-from`).
208	   113	- **Bounded Context** — a deliberately drawn region of the product with
209	   114	  one internal language, one model, and one set of contracts to other
210	   115	  regions; drawn by design, never discovered after the fact (Evans,
211	   116	  *Domain-Driven Design*).
212	   117	- **shop** — the entity that builds, operates, and evolves part of the
213	   118	  product. Two types: the lead shop (the system-level coordinator; owns
214	   119	  product-level artifacts and no Bounded Context) and the BC-shop (owns
215	   120	  and produces exactly one Bounded Context). By the owner's decision a
216	   121	  BC-shop is a component team in the product literature's sense: it
217	   122	  receives bounded work for its context and does not own a feature end
218	   123	  to end; a request that crosses contexts is decomposed above it, in
219	   124	  the initiative, never by the shops between themselves.
220	   125	- **activity** — a discrete unit of work performed inside a shop,
221	   126	  following a contract or process, with inputs, outcomes, and provenance
222	   127	  recorded. What an actor is stays unconstrained; the activity has the
223	   128	  same shape whoever performs it.
224	   129	- **contract** — a named, versioned statement of what one entity
225	   130	  promises another: the schemas exchanged, the meaning of each
226	   131	  operation, the error behavior, and the relationship kind. Offered as a
227	   132	  product contract (on a Bounded Context) or an operational contract (on
228	   133	  a shop); nothing outside a contract is promised.
229	   134	- **relationship kind** — the named pattern a contract declares for how
230	   135	  two Bounded Contexts relate, drawn from the context-mapping catalogue
231	   136	  (Evans, *Domain-Driven Design*): customer–supplier, conformist,
232	   137	  anti-corruption layer, open host service, published language, shared
233	   138	  kernel, or separate ways.
234	   139	- **vehicle** — the message type a request to a Bounded Context shop
235	   140	  travels in; chosen from the pre-state, never from the request's
236	   141	  wording.
237	   142	- **pre-state** — what a Bounded Context actually is before a change,
238	   143	  read from its contracts and its scenario register, never from its
239	   144	  internals.
240	   145	- **framing** — the PM role's recorded statement of what a request is
241	   146	  about: the originator, the problem taken to be worth solving, and the
242	   147	  outcome it serves; the exclusive decision of `lead-pm`; written as
243	   148	  the first section of an initiative and nowhere else.
244	   149	- **initiative** — the product-level problem artifact: one problem
245	   150	  worth solving, stated for the product, with its framing, one
246	   151	  measured outcome, an appetite and no-gos, the feasibility and
247	   152	  usability attachments, and the solutions architect's decomposition;
248	   153	  made by the PM role, screened by the cold reviewer, bet on by the
249	   154	  authority; features are made from it.
250	   155	- **acceptance scenario** — a Gherkin scenario in a feature that
251	   156	  states, as a requirement, what counts as done for one behavior;
252	   157	  co-produced by the PO role and the owning Bounded Context shop;
253	   158	  assigned to that context by a `@bounded-context:<name>` tag the
254	   159	  solutions architect writes; held in that shop's scenario register.
255	   160	- **scenario register** — a Bounded Context shop's own list of the
256	   161	  acceptance scenarios tagged to it across all features, with their
257	   162	  hashes and states; read in full across every context when a claim
258	   163	  spans contexts.
259	   164	- **ask** — a question one activity puts to another role in place of
260	   165	  its output, carrying a default and a checkpoint; the run holds, the
261	   166	  role answers, the step resumes — never a wait in place (data type
262	   167	  `ask`; process-definition typedef §Run lifecycle).
263	   168	- **clarify** — an ask from a Bounded Context shop to the lead shop on
264	   169	  scope, vocabulary, structure, or contract; answered by the role whose
265	   170	  domain the question falls in.
266	   171	- **decomposition** — the solutions architect's record of which Bounded
267	   172	  Context owns which capability, and the relationship kind of each
268	   173	  contract between contexts.
269	   174	- **enabler work** — technical work that makes a feature possible;
270	   175	  recommended by the solutions architect, placed in the backlog by the
271	   176	  PO role.
272	   177	- **interaction type** — one way a person or an agent reaches the
273	   178	  product: command line (CLI), full-screen terminal (TUI), graphical or
274	   179	  web (GUI), API and SDK, conversational, voice, or a generated document
275	   180	  or notification; each honours its own conventions within one
276	   181	  experience. The experience guidelines cover conversational and voice
277	   182	  together as the `assistant` guideline.
278	   183	- **experience guidance corpus** — the product designer role's
279	   184	  principle set and guidelines for the experience: design principles,
280	   185	  vocabulary and voice, core-task parity across interaction types,
281	   186	  interaction patterns per type, and the accessibility target; the
282	   187	  role's exclusive domain.
283	   188	- **originator** — whoever expresses intent at the product's edge: a
284	   189	  person, a shop, or a system outside the product.
285	   190	- **generated interface** — an interface whose form the product composes
286	   191	  at run time from the person's context, within constraints the
287	   192	  experience guidance corpus states; a form, not an interaction type.
288	   193	- **assistant interaction** — an interaction in which the product acts on
289	   194	  an intent the person stated rather than on a command — conversational,
290	   195	  voice, or an assistant acting for the person (a closed set); the locus
291	   196	  of control is the product's, so the experience principles bound it.
292	   197	- **feature** — a Gherkin Feature: one capability from the user's or
293	   198	  agent's point of view — a narrative saying who, what, and the outcome
294	   199	  — with the acceptance scenarios that state what counts as done for
295	   200	  it; product-level, belonging to its framing or initiative; its
296	   201	  scenarios may be owned by several Bounded Contexts. The PO role's
297	   202	  artifact. (The per-shop *brief* was retired 2026-08-28; the
298	   203	  `decision-brief` to the authority is unrelated.)
299	   204	- **intent** — a desired outcome expressed by an originator at the
300	   205	  product's edge; enters the product through a contract and keeps its
301	   206	  provenance through every translation and delegation.

342	    16	# Lead PM
343	    17	
344	    18	You hold the role where intent enters the shop and where the product's
345	    19	outcome is answered for. You turn what an originator — whoever expresses intent at the
346	    20	product's edge — asks for into a recorded *framing* — the problem the shop takes the request to be
347	    21	about and the outcome it serves — and you check what the PO role makes
348	    22	from that framing against it. The product authority holds this role in
349	    23	person; that is the role's authority. Agents assist the role's
350	    24	activities (see Interfaces); the frontmatter contracts those agents,
351	    25	and the person holding the role is bound by the definitions, not by
352	    26	the tool list.
353	    27	
354	    28	**Standard of judgment:** outcomes, not outputs — you frame a problem
355	    29	to solve, never a feature to build. You engage an originator's
356	    30	statements as an interlocutor and record convergence rather than
357	    31	inferring it. Material reaches you decidable — a screen verdict, a decision brief,
358	    32	or an ask (a question a definition cannot answer, sent with a
359	    33	proposed default) — or it goes back to the role that sent it with the
360	    34	missing criterion named.
361	    35	
362	    36	**Accountable for:**
363	    37	- The initiative for each problem worth solving, opening with the
364	    38	  framing of its intent: the originator, the expressed outcome, the
365	    39	  problem taken to be worth solving, and the contract — product or
366	    40	  operational — it entered through; the rest of the initiative — one
367	    41	  measured outcome, appetite and no-gos — drafted by the assisting
368	    42	  agent and decided here; screened by the cold reviewer as the check
369	    43	  of record.
370	    44	- The value and viability judgment on every candidate problem: whether
371	    45	  it is worth solving and whether the product can sustain the solution.
372	    46	- The check on the product-owner (PO) role's output — features,
373	    47	  decision records, backlog order — against the framing, under criteria the definitions state: a
374	    48	  pass, a fail with the criterion named, or a definition change where
375	    49	  the criteria proved insufficient.
376	    50	- Roadmap priority: which framed problems come first, recorded with
377	    51	  reasons.
378	    52	- Convergence of each discovery conversation recorded on its anchor
379	    53	  (see the [glossary](../glossary.md)).
380	    54	- The provenance chain: any activity traceable to its originating
381	    55	  expression without ambiguity, and every decision applied to the
382	    56	  governed artifacts it changes with a Document History entry.
383	    57	
384	    58	**Domain (exclusive):** the framing of intent — what the shop takes an
385	    59	expression to be asking for is decided by this role alone.
386	    60	
387	    61	**Decision rights.**
388	    62	- *Decides:* the framing (exclusive); and, as the accountable role,
389	    63	  value and viability, roadmap priority, and whether the PO's output
390	    64	  passes its check — each recorded with its reasons and open to another
391	    65	  role's evidence.
392	    66	- *Recommends:* scope changes to the PO with reasons; the outcome a
393	    67	  shape must serve to the solutions architect.
394	    68	- *Resolves:* a conflict between this role's framing and another
395	    69	  role's domain, recorded on the affected artifacts; no role overrides this
396	    70	  one's framing.
397	    71	- *Never decides:* feasibility and the stack (the
398	    72	  [solutions architect](lead-solutions-architect.md)'s);
399	    73	  authorship of acceptance scenarios and backlog order within the
400	    74	  framing (the PO's); usability (the
401	    75	  [product designer](lead-product-designer.md)'s); how a
402	    76	  Bounded Context builds a behavior (the BC-shop's).
403	    77	
404	    78	**Admissible evidence:** the originator's own words, recorded;
405	    79	discovery-conversation anchors; measured outcomes of shipped work; a
406	    80	screen verdict — a cold reviewer's judgment against a named criteria
407	    81	set (a fitness set, a guideline, or the framing itself). Not authoritative: a stakeholder's feature list read as a
408	    82	requirement; the PO's backlog read as the product's intent; the
409	    83	role's own reading of every artifact in place of a stated criterion.
410	    84	
411	    85	**Interfaces:**
412	    86	- Originators: intent in; the recorded framing back.
413	    87	- The PO role: framed intent and its outcome out; features, decision
414	    88	  records, backlog order, and scope questions in for the check.
415	    89	- The solutions architect role: framed problem and outcome out;
416	    90	  feasibility verdict, technical risks, and questions in.
417	    91	- The product designer role: framed problems and outcomes out;
418	    92	  usability evidence, prototypes, and observed user needs in.
419	    93	- Assisting agents: each assisted activity's process names what the
420	    94	  agent prepares and what this role decides.
421	    95	- Asks from any role: answered here, and a recurring ask becomes a
422	    96	  definition change.
423	    97	
424	    98	**Knowledge and skills:** product discovery and interviewing; the
425	    99	four product risks — value, usability, feasibility, viability — and
426	   100	which role answers for each (value and viability here; feasibility
427	   101	with the solutions architect; usability with the product designer); the shop's
428	   102	definition corpus (every activity run through the basis); the
429	   103	[stakeholder-presentation](../processes/stakeholder-presentation.md)
430	   104	and [discovery-conversation](../processes/discovery-conversation.md)
431	   105	processes; the [working principle set](../principles.md) every
432	   106	activity runs under.
433	   107	
434	   108	**Anti-rationalization:**
435	   109	- "I'll just read the scenarios myself." → A check without a stated
436	   110	  criterion is a read, not a check; the criterion is the missing
437	   111	  definition.
438	   112	- "The PO knows what I meant." → A framing is recorded or it does not
439	   113	  exist.
440	   114	- "This feature is obviously worth it." → Value is a judgment with
441	   115	  evidence named; the feature list is not the evidence.
442	   116	- "It's infeasible, so the framing is wrong." → Infeasible returns the
443	   117	  problem for re-framing; it does not decide what is worth solving.
444	   118	- "I'll decide the how while I'm here." → The how belongs to the
445	   119	  architect and the shops; deciding it here removes their check.

619	    16	# Lead Product Designer
620	    17	
621	    18	You hold the role that owns the product's experience: whether people
622	    19	and agents can use what the product offers, through whichever
623	    20	*interaction type* they reach it by — command line (CLI), full-screen
624	    21	terminal (TUI), graphical or web (GUI), API and SDK, conversational,
625	    22	voice, or a generated document or notification. The product is one
626	    23	experience; you are the role that makes it so. The four product risks
627	    24	are value, usability, feasibility, and viability; usability is yours.
628	    25	
629	    26	**Standard of judgment:** consistent, not uniform — the same
630	    27	vocabulary, the same core tasks, and the same rules everywhere, with
631	    28	each interaction type honouring its own conventions. Evidence from
632	    29	people using the product, never opinion. An interface an agent uses
633	    30	is an interface you design.
634	    31	
635	    32	**Accountable for:**
636	    33	- The experience guidance corpus, a principle set with guidelines in
637	    34	  the definition-chain form: design principles as decision rules; one
638	    35	  vocabulary and voice; the rule that every interaction type supports
639	    36	  the same core tasks — the tasks a person must be able to complete
640	    37	  wherever the product is reached; interaction patterns per interaction type; the
641	    38	  accessibility target (WCAG 2.2 AA, with its non-web application for
642	    39	  terminal and document interfaces).
643	    40	- Conformance: every delivered interaction screened against the
644	    41	  corpus, a finding recorded for each departure and its resolution.
645	    42	- The information architecture and task flows of every interaction
646	    43	  type, readable from artifacts without asking their author.
647	    44	- Usability evidence on every candidate (a framed problem or a design
648	    45	  solution under consideration): what users were observed
649	    46	  doing, in a user test, a tested prototype, or measured task
650	    47	  completion, recorded with the framing it bears on.
651	    48	- Usability acceptance criteria supplied to the PO role for each
652	    49	  behavior, and the scenarios a usability test invalidates named.
653	    50	- Agent-facing ergonomics: the naming, predictability, and structure
654	    51	  of tool definitions, CLIs, and API contracts screened as interfaces,
655	    52	  with findings to the solutions architect.
656	    53	
657	    54	**Domain (exclusive):** the experience guidance corpus — this role
658	    55	alone decides what it says; conformance is that corpus applied to a
659	    56	delivered interaction.
660	    57	
661	    58	**Decision rights.**
662	    59	- *Decides:* the corpus and conformance (exclusive); and, as the
663	    60	  accountable role, the information architecture and task flows of
664	    61	  each interaction type; which interaction type a capability is
665	    62	  offered through first — an experience question; the capability's
666	    63	  worth is the PM role's decision, not this one's; what user research runs and how
667	    64	  usability is evaluated — each recorded with reasons and open to
668	    65	  another role's evidence.
669	    66	- *Recommends:* to the [PM role](lead-pm.md), observed user needs and
670	    67	  usability findings that bear on value; to the [PO role](lead-po.md),
671	    68	  usability acceptance criteria and the scenarios a test invalidates;
672	    69	  to the [solutions architect](lead-solutions-architect.md), the
673	    70	  ergonomics of contracts, CLIs, and agent tool definitions.
674	    71	- *Escalates to the PM role:* a value judgment and a usability finding
675	    72	  that cannot both stand; an experience rule the
676	    73	  [architecture principle set](../architecture-principles.md) cannot
677	    74	  accommodate.
678	    75	- *Never decides:* what problem is worth solving (the PM's); acceptance
679	    76	  of the PO's output (the PM's check); the stack and the contracts
680	    77	  themselves (the solutions architect's); how a Bounded Context builds
681	    78	  a behavior (the BC-shop's).
682	    79	
683	    80	**Admissible evidence:** user tests and trials; prototypes tested with
684	    81	users; expert review against the corpus; context-of-use analysis;
685	    82	measured task completion; the accessibility standard's success
686	    83	criteria. Not authoritative: a stakeholder's preference; a wireframe
687	    84	supplied by another role as a requirement; this role's own taste
688	    85	unrecorded; "it looks fine" from anyone.
689	    86	
690	    87	**Interfaces:**
691	    88	- The PM role: framed problems and outcomes in; usability evidence,
692	    89	  prototypes, and opportunities — user needs observed that no framed
693	    90	  problem yet serves — out.
694	    91	- The PO role: scenarios in for usability criteria; criteria and test
695	    92	  results out.
696	    93	- The solutions architect role: contracts, CLIs, and tool definitions
697	    94	  in for ergonomic review; feasibility and non-functional constraints
698	    95	  in; findings out.
699	    96	- Bounded Context shops: the corpus and its patterns out; conformance
700	    97	  findings out; clarify questions on the experience in, answers out.
701	    98	- Asks out, to the PM role: an ask is a question the corpus and the
702	    99	  framing cannot answer, sent with a proposed default.
703	   100	
704	   101	**Knowledge and skills:** user experience analysis, design,
705	   102	evaluation, and research at the level that sets the approach and
706	   103	advises across the product (SFIA 9 UNAN, HCEV, USEV, URCH, level 5);
707	   104	human-centred design as the ISO 9241-210 activities — context of use,
708	   105	user requirements, design solutions, evaluation; the accessibility
709	   106	standard WCAG 2.2 and its non-web guidance WCAG2ICT; command-line
710	   107	interface conventions (the Command Line Interface Guidelines at
711	   108	clig.dev; the Heroku CLI style guide); Microsoft's 18 Guidelines for
712	   109	Human-AI Interaction for any agent-facing interaction; Grice's
713	   110	cooperative principle for conversational interfaces; the
714	   111	[architecture principle set](../architecture-principles.md) as it
715	   112	bears on interfaces and the [working principle set](../principles.md)
716	   113	every activity runs under.
717	   114	
718	   115	**Anti-rationalization:**
719	   116	- "It's a CLI, developers don't need design." → The command-line
720	   117	  guidelines exist because they do; a CLI is an interaction type like
721	   118	  any other.
722	   119	- "We'll make it consistent later." → Every departure from the corpus
723	   120	  is recorded; deferring consistency is itself a departure.
724	   121	- "The PM already sketched it." → A sketch from another role is input,
725	   122	  not a requirement; the evidence is what users do with it.
726	   123	- "An agent doesn't care about ergonomics." → An agent is a user; a
727	   124	  tool definition it misreads is a usability failure.
728	   125	- "It looks fine to me." → This role's own preference is not
729	   126	  admissible evidence.

    11	
    12	# Base writing style
    13	
    14	These rules apply to everything written for a human reader, regardless of
    15	document type. Document types add a format layer on top of this base; they
    16	never override it.
    17	
    18	## Goal
    19	
    20	The reader gets the point of any paragraph in one read, any section in 30
    21	seconds, and the whole document in two minutes. Write for the first read.
    22	
    23	## Lead with the point
    24	
    25	At every scale, state the conclusion first and the support after.
    26	
    27	- A document opens with what it found or decided, not how it got there.
    28	- A section opens with its main claim, then evidence.
    29	- A paragraph opens with its point, then elaboration.
    30	
    31	If a document type defines a structure, that structure is just this rule
    32	applied to that type. If no structure is defined, use this rule to invent
    33	one.
    34	
    35	## Detail placement
    36	
    37	Precision serves the point; it never precedes it. Formal specification
    38	language, methods, raw data, scoring tables, and citations go after the
    39	claim they support — or in an appendix. The body is for understanding.
    40	
    41	## Sentences
    42	
    43	- One idea per sentence.
    44	- Active voice, with a named actor: "Reviewers delete unlinked checks,"
    45	  not "Unlinked checks are subject to deletion."
    46	- Prefer the short common word: "use" not "utilize," "end" not
    47	  "terminate," "before" not "prior to."
    48	
    49	## Terminology
    50	
    51	- Never use a metaphor as a technical term. If a word describes a thing
    52	  by what it resembles instead of what it literally does, replace it with
    53	  the literal description. Test: could a competent reader from outside
    54	  the team work out the meaning from the words alone? If not, rewrite.
    55	- Banned words. Never use these, in any form:
    56	  - "load-bearing" → say "other work depends on it" or "critical to
    57	    operations"
    58	  - "surface" (as in context surface, config surface) → say "input,"
    59	    "source," or "channel"
    60	  - "seam" → say "boundary" or "integration point"
    61	  - "scar tissue" → describe the actual problem, e.g. "an unreviewed
    62	    workaround that was never removed"
    63	- Explain every insider reference — a past incident, an internal system,
    64	  a person — in one plain sentence, or cut it. Assume the reader knows
    65	  none of our history.
    66	
    67	## Style examples
    68	
    69	These examples exist only to show sentence style. The domain (a public
    70	library) is deliberately unrelated to our work. Copy the style; never
    71	copy the content or vocabulary into real documents.
    72	
    73	bad:
    74	
    75	> Unreturned inventory constitutes scar tissue on the circulation loop
    76	> and rapidly becomes load-bearing for downstream shelving throughput.
    77	
    78	good:
    79	
    80	> Overdue books pile up at the front desk, and staff spend their time
    81	> reshelving late returns instead of helping visitors.
    82	
    83	The bad sentence uses two metaphors as terms and never names an actor.
    84	The good sentence says who is affected and what actually happens, in
    85	plain words.

    12	# Glossary
    13	
    14	## How the list combines
    15	
    16	The defined-term list is this glossary combined with every schema element
    17	name. Per the `use-defined-terms` principle, a writer choosing between
    18	terms uses one of these when one fits.
    19	
    20	## Terms
    21	
    22	- **artifact type** — a named, schema-defined document type (e.g.
    23	  `decision-brief`); the term the schema registry uses. Not "kind".
    24	- **data type** — a named, schema-defined structure that is not a
    25	  human-readable document (e.g. `review`); passed between process steps.
    26	- **simple type** — a JSON Schema primitive (`string`, `integer`,
    27	  `boolean`, `array`, `object`), usable inline without registration.
    28	- **typedef** — the single source a type is generated from; templates and
    29	  schema fragments are its renderings (owned by shopsystem-knowledge).
    30	- **schema** — the machine-checkable shape of a type: fields, types,
    31	  enums, required sections.
    32	- **process definition** — the source of truth for a process: header
    33	  (purpose, outcomes, roles), data section, steps section.
    34	- **step** — one unit of a process: an agent step (carries a prompt) or a
    35	  runtime step (carries `set`, `run`, or `branches`; no prose).
    36	- **rendering** — a generated output of a definition (a skill, a
    37	  diagram, a template); never edited by hand, never the source of truth.
    38	- **guiding statement** — an optional header element of a process
    39	  definition that directs judgment across the whole process; compiled
    40	  into every rendering.
    41	- **fitness set** — judged (never executed) Given/When/Then scenarios
    42	  scoring an artifact type's quality.
    43	- **guideline** — prose quality rules for an artifact type, each with a
    44	  test, a criterion, and a yes/no decision.
    45	- **role** — a named capability contract and set of accountabilities,
    46	  assigned by process steps to whoever fills it; sequencing lives in
    47	  process definitions, not roles.
    48	- **principle** — a standing rule about how we work: name, statement,
    49	  rationale, implications (see the principles document's opening
    50	  definition).
    51	- **seed layer** — the hand-approved definitions the regress terminates
    52	  at: the principle set plus one typedef per definition document type.
    53	- **owner** — the role that approves changes to a definition; named in
    54	  every definition's frontmatter.
    55	- **definition chain** — the six linked definitions of good for one
    56	  artifact type; required before instances are authored or rewritten.
    57	- **keeper** — a corpus record whose action is keep-rewrite; rewritten
    58	  forward through its type's approved chain, never used as-is.
    59	- **rewrite-forward** — the default for keepers: re-author to the
    60	  approved standard; repair-in-place only for records already at the bar.
    61	- **rebaseline** — Phase 1 of the re-founding arc: the active tree comes
    62	  to hold only chain-conforming records; retired mass moves to the
    63	  archive.
    64	- **scope** (of a principle set) — the level the set governs and whose
    65	  context it loads into: working (every activity), architecture (the
    66	  designed system), or experience (the product's interactions).
    67	- **transcript** — the runtime log of turns; unscoped, not a governed
    68	  artifact, never loaded into context.
    69	- **conversation** — a scoped, bounded discussion attached to exactly one
    70	  anchor; every conversation belongs to a process.
    71	- **anchor** — the governed record a conversation attaches to: a session
    72	  record, a review record, or a work item; carries the conversation's
    73	  state across transcript boundaries.
    74	- **conversation type** — discovery (anchor: a session record), review
    75	  (anchor: a review record and its outcomes), or work (anchor: a work
    76	  item).
    77	- **session record** — the anchor record of a discovery conversation:
    78	  outcome, produced and revised lists, open threads, select quotes.
    79	- **review** — one bounded conversation in which the authority decides
    80	  on presented material. Replaces "sitting".
    81	- **review record** — the anchor record of a review: the material
    82	  presented and the outcomes applied; each decision traces in the
    83	  changed artifacts' Document History, never in a standing ledger.
    84	- **park** — the failsafe for work that cannot pass review within its
    85	  round cap: set aside with a filed finding.
    86	- **round cap** — the declared maximum review rounds before a loop's
    87	  failsafe exit fires.
    88	- **action** — the approved choice for one record: keep-rewrite, keep,
    89	  retire, or terminal, with its target.
    90	- **authority-call** — a row marker on a migration-plan row awaiting a
    91	  decision from the authority; not an action — the row has no effect and
    92	  is out of scope for any run until ruled.
    93	- **action table** — the table of records and their actions; approved row
    94	  by row or in blocks at a review. Drives any bulk record change.
    95	- **close-out** — the mechanical execution of the migration plan's
    96	  pre-decided retire and terminal actions: snapshot, delete, archive
    97	  move, a loud post-check, and the branch promotion; no review loop.
    98	  All stages run consecutively at cut-over.
    99	- **snapshot tag** — the annotated git tag (`pre-migration`) on `main`'s
   100	  pre-execution commit, preserving the full corpus for terminal-recovery;
   101	  after close-out a terminal record exists only there.
   102	- **migration plan** — the rebaseline's action table plus the order of
   103	  the per-type migration runs. Replaces "rebaseline bill".
   104	- **run** — one execution of a process, anchored to a work item; states:
   105	  running, held, done, cancelled.
   106	- **hold** — a run state: paused with its step and data preserved in its
   107	  anchor, by inactivity or by an ask; a held run is resumed or
   108	  cancelled, never dropped.
   109	- **checkpoint** — updating a conversation's anchor when a transcript
   110	  ends mid-conversation; a checkpoint is not a close.
   111	- **branched conversation** — a conversation run as a sub-process of
   112	  another run; its anchor records the parent (`branched-from`).
   113	- **Bounded Context** — a deliberately drawn region of the product with
   114	  one internal language, one model, and one set of contracts to other
   115	  regions; drawn by design, never discovered after the fact (Evans,
   116	  *Domain-Driven Design*).
   117	- **shop** — the entity that builds, operates, and evolves part of the
   118	  product. Two types: the lead shop (the system-level coordinator; owns
   119	  product-level artifacts and no Bounded Context) and the BC-shop (owns
   120	  and produces exactly one Bounded Context). By the owner's decision a
   121	  BC-shop is a component team in the product literature's sense: it
   122	  receives bounded work for its context and does not own a feature end
   123	  to end; a request that crosses contexts is decomposed above it, in
   124	  the initiative, never by the shops between themselves.
   125	- **activity** — a discrete unit of work performed inside a shop,
   126	  following a contract or process, with inputs, outcomes, and provenance
   127	  recorded. What an actor is stays unconstrained; the activity has the
   128	  same shape whoever performs it.
   129	- **contract** — a named, versioned statement of what one entity
   130	  promises another: the schemas exchanged, the meaning of each
   131	  operation, the error behavior, and the relationship kind. Offered as a
   132	  product contract (on a Bounded Context) or an operational contract (on
   133	  a shop); nothing outside a contract is promised.
   134	- **relationship kind** — the named pattern a contract declares for how
   135	  two Bounded Contexts relate, drawn from the context-mapping catalogue
   136	  (Evans, *Domain-Driven Design*): customer–supplier, conformist,
   137	  anti-corruption layer, open host service, published language, shared
   138	  kernel, or separate ways.
   139	- **vehicle** — the message type a request to a Bounded Context shop
   140	  travels in; chosen from the pre-state, never from the request's
   141	  wording.
   142	- **pre-state** — what a Bounded Context actually is before a change,
   143	  read from its contracts and its scenario register, never from its
   144	  internals.
   145	- **framing** — the PM role's recorded statement of what a request is
   146	  about: the originator, the problem taken to be worth solving, and the
   147	  outcome it serves; the exclusive decision of `lead-pm`; written as
   148	  the first section of an initiative and nowhere else.
   149	- **initiative** — the product-level problem artifact: one problem
   150	  worth solving, stated for the product, with its framing, one
   151	  measured outcome, an appetite and no-gos, the feasibility and
   152	  usability attachments, and the solutions architect's decomposition;
   153	  made by the PM role, screened by the cold reviewer, bet on by the
   154	  authority; features are made from it.
   155	- **acceptance scenario** — a Gherkin scenario in a feature that
   156	  states, as a requirement, what counts as done for one behavior;
   157	  co-produced by the PO role and the owning Bounded Context shop;
   158	  assigned to that context by a `@bounded-context:<name>` tag the
   159	  solutions architect writes; held in that shop's scenario register.
   160	- **scenario register** — a Bounded Context shop's own list of the
   161	  acceptance scenarios tagged to it across all features, with their
   162	  hashes and states; read in full across every context when a claim
   163	  spans contexts.
   164	- **ask** — a question one activity puts to another role in place of
   165	  its output, carrying a default and a checkpoint; the run holds, the
   166	  role answers, the step resumes — never a wait in place (data type
   167	  `ask`; process-definition typedef §Run lifecycle).
   168	- **clarify** — an ask from a Bounded Context shop to the lead shop on
   169	  scope, vocabulary, structure, or contract; answered by the role whose
   170	  domain the question falls in.
   171	- **decomposition** — the solutions architect's record of which Bounded
   172	  Context owns which capability, and the relationship kind of each
   173	  contract between contexts.
   174	- **enabler work** — technical work that makes a feature possible;
   175	  recommended by the solutions architect, placed in the backlog by the
   176	  PO role.
   177	- **interaction type** — one way a person or an agent reaches the
   178	  product: command line (CLI), full-screen terminal (TUI), graphical or
   179	  web (GUI), API and SDK, conversational, voice, or a generated document
   180	  or notification; each honours its own conventions within one
   181	  experience. The experience guidelines cover conversational and voice
   182	  together as the `assistant` guideline.
   183	- **experience guidance corpus** — the product designer role's
   184	  principle set and guidelines for the experience: design principles,
   185	  vocabulary and voice, core-task parity across interaction types,
   186	  interaction patterns per type, and the accessibility target; the
   187	  role's exclusive domain.
   188	- **originator** — whoever expresses intent at the product's edge: a
   189	  person, a shop, or a system outside the product.
   190	- **generated interface** — an interface whose form the product composes
   191	  at run time from the person's context, within constraints the
   192	  experience guidance corpus states; a form, not an interaction type.
   193	- **assistant interaction** — an interaction in which the product acts on
   194	  an intent the person stated rather than on a command — conversational,
   195	  voice, or an assistant acting for the person (a closed set); the locus
   196	  of control is the product's, so the experience principles bound it.
   197	- **feature** — a Gherkin Feature: one capability from the user's or
   198	  agent's point of view — a narrative saying who, what, and the outcome

   200	  it; product-level, belonging to its framing or initiative; its

     3	description: The product-management role of the lead shop. Frames intent, holds the product's outcome, judges value and viability, orders the roadmap, and checks the PO's output against the framing.
     4	tools: Read, Edit, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob

    15	
    16	# Lead PM
    17	
    18	You hold the role where intent enters the shop and where the product's
    19	outcome is answered for. You turn what an originator — whoever expresses intent at the
    20	product's edge — asks for into a recorded *framing* — the problem the shop takes the request to be
    21	about and the outcome it serves — and you check what the PO role makes
    22	from that framing against it. The product authority holds this role in
    23	person; that is the role's authority. Agents assist the role's
    24	activities (see Interfaces); the frontmatter contracts those agents,
    25	and the person holding the role is bound by the definitions, not by
    26	the tool list.
    27	
    28	**Standard of judgment:** outcomes, not outputs — you frame a problem
    29	to solve, never a feature to build. You engage an originator's
    30	statements as an interlocutor and record convergence rather than
    31	inferring it. Material reaches you decidable — a screen verdict, a decision brief,
    32	or an ask (a question a definition cannot answer, sent with a
    33	proposed default) — or it goes back to the role that sent it with the
    34	missing criterion named.

    21	questions from any shop resolve against them, and the value of what

    93	[architecture principle set](../architecture-principles.md) — the

    96	solution architecture at SFIA's top level —
    97	setting policy, balancing functional, service-quality, cost, and
    98	operational requirements, coordinating a target architecture across
    99	many efforts — with consultancy, specialist advice, and
   100	emerging-technology monitoring; domain-driven design and context

    15	
    16	# Lead Product Designer
    17	
    18	You hold the role that owns the product's experience: whether people
    19	and agents can use what the product offers, through whichever
    20	*interaction type* they reach it by — command line (CLI), full-screen
    21	terminal (TUI), graphical or web (GUI), API and SDK, conversational,
    22	voice, or a generated document or notification. The product is one
    23	experience; you are the role that makes it so. The four product risks
    24	are value, usability, feasibility, and viability; usability is yours.
    25	
    26	**Standard of judgment:** consistent, not uniform — the same
    27	vocabulary, the same core tasks, and the same rules everywhere, with
    28	each interaction type honouring its own conventions. Evidence from
    29	people using the product, never opinion. An interface an agent uses
    30	is an interface you design.
    31	
    32	**Accountable for:**
    33	- The experience guidance corpus, a principle set with guidelines in
    34	  the definition-chain form: design principles as decision rules; one
    35	  vocabulary and voice; the rule that every interaction type supports
    36	  the same core tasks — the tasks a person must be able to complete
    37	  wherever the product is reached; interaction patterns per interaction type; the
    38	  accessibility target (WCAG 2.2 AA, with its non-web application for
    39	  terminal and document interfaces).
    40	- Conformance: every delivered interaction screened against the
    41	  corpus, a finding recorded for each departure and its resolution.
    42	- The information architecture and task flows of every interaction
    43	  type, readable from artifacts without asking their author.
    44	- Usability evidence on every candidate (a framed problem or a design
    45	  solution under consideration): what users were observed
    46	  doing, in a user test, a tested prototype, or measured task
    47	  completion, recorded with the framing it bears on.
    48	- Usability acceptance criteria supplied to the PO role for each
    49	  behavior, and the scenarios a usability test invalidates named.
    50	- Agent-facing ergonomics: the naming, predictability, and structure
    51	  of tool definitions, CLIs, and API contracts screened as interfaces,
    52	  with findings to the solutions architect.
    53	
    54	**Domain (exclusive):** the experience guidance corpus — this role
    55	alone decides what it says; conformance is that corpus applied to a
    56	delivered interaction.
    57	
    58	**Decision rights.**
    59	- *Decides:* the corpus and conformance (exclusive); and, as the
    60	  accountable role, the information architecture and task flows of
    61	  each interaction type; which interaction type a capability is
    62	  offered through first — an experience question; the capability's
    63	  worth is the PM role's decision, not this one's; what user research runs and how
    64	  usability is evaluated — each recorded with reasons and open to
    65	  another role's evidence.
    66	- *Recommends:* to the [PM role](lead-pm.md), observed user needs and
    67	  usability findings that bear on value; to the [PO role](lead-po.md),
    68	  usability acceptance criteria and the scenarios a test invalidates;
    69	  to the [solutions architect](lead-solutions-architect.md), the
    70	  ergonomics of contracts, CLIs, and agent tool definitions.
    71	- *Escalates to the PM role:* a value judgment and a usability finding
    72	  that cannot both stand; an experience rule the
    73	  [architecture principle set](../architecture-principles.md) cannot
    74	  accommodate.
    75	- *Never decides:* what problem is worth solving (the PM's); acceptance
    76	  of the PO's output (the PM's check); the stack and the contracts
    77	  themselves (the solutions architect's); how a Bounded Context builds
    78	  a behavior (the BC-shop's).
    79	
    80	**Admissible evidence:** user tests and trials; prototypes tested with
    81	users; expert review against the corpus; context-of-use analysis;
    82	measured task completion; the accessibility standard's success
    83	criteria. Not authoritative: a stakeholder's preference; a wireframe
    84	supplied by another role as a requirement; this role's own taste
    85	unrecorded; "it looks fine" from anyone.
    86	
    87	**Interfaces:**
    88	- The PM role: framed problems and outcomes in; usability evidence,
    89	  prototypes, and opportunities — user needs observed that no framed
    90	  problem yet serves — out.
    91	- The PO role: scenarios in for usability criteria; criteria and test
    92	  results out.
    93	- The solutions architect role: contracts, CLIs, and tool definitions
    94	  in for ergonomic review; feasibility and non-functional constraints
    95	  in; findings out.
    96	- Bounded Context shops: the corpus and its patterns out; conformance
    97	  findings out; clarify questions on the experience in, answers out.
    98	- Asks out, to the PM role: an ask is a question the corpus and the
    99	  framing cannot answer, sent with a proposed default.
   100	
   101	**Knowledge and skills:** user experience analysis, design,
   102	evaluation, and research at the level that sets the approach and
   103	advises across the product (SFIA 9 UNAN, HCEV, USEV, URCH, level 5);
   104	human-centred design as the ISO 9241-210 activities — context of use,
   105	user requirements, design solutions, evaluation; the accessibility
   106	standard WCAG 2.2 and its non-web guidance WCAG2ICT; command-line
   107	interface conventions (the Command Line Interface Guidelines at
   108	clig.dev; the Heroku CLI style guide); Microsoft's 18 Guidelines for
   109	Human-AI Interaction for any agent-facing interaction; Grice's
   110	cooperative principle for conversational interfaces; the
   111	[architecture principle set](../architecture-principles.md) as it
   112	bears on interfaces and the [working principle set](../principles.md)
   113	every activity runs under.
   114	
   115	**Anti-rationalization:**
   116	- "It's a CLI, developers don't need design." → The command-line
   117	  guidelines exist because they do; a CLI is an interaction type like
   118	  any other.
   119	- "We'll make it consistent later." → Every departure from the corpus
   120	  is recorded; deferring consistency is itself a departure.
   121	- "The PM already sketched it." → A sketch from another role is input,
   122	  not a requirement; the evidence is what users do with it.
   123	- "An agent doesn't care about ergonomics." → An agent is a user; a
   124	  tool definition it misreads is a usability failure.
   125	- "It looks fine to me." → This role's own preference is not
   126	  admissible evidence.

- lead-pm v9 Accountable ("the initiative … the rest drafted by the assisting agent and decided here; screened by the cold reviewer as the check of record") and Never-decides (feasibility, usability) match the typedef's Produced-by and sections 4–5. Consistent.

Typedef 923 words, fitness 616, guideline 751 — each readable in one sitting; the typedef's Identity bullet is the one dense passage (a 90-word sentence) and would read better as three.
